objectives: Master contract formation + UCC Article 2 + remedies (Hadley v Baxendale).
Explain estates, easements, zoning, + takings (Euclid, Kelo, Lucas).
Apply negligence, products liability, + defamation doctrine.

slides.title: Contracts: formation, UCC, + remedies
slides.body:
**Contract law** governs voluntary obligation-creation through promise. The American common law of contracts derives from the English tradition (medieval forms of action through Holmes + the **Restatement (Second) of Contracts** (1981; Allan Farnsworth Reporter)) + is supplemented by the **Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)** — particularly **Article 2 (Sales)** for goods — drafted by **Karl Llewellyn** + the American Law Institute + the Uniform Law Commission (1952; widely enacted 1960s; revised periodically).

**Formation requires** offer, acceptance, + consideration:
- **Offer** — manifestation of willingness to enter into a bargain, justifying offeree's belief that assent is invited + would conclude the bargain. *Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store* (1957) — advertisement as offer when sufficiently definite. Revocation generally permitted before acceptance (*Dickinson v. Dodds* 1876).
- **Acceptance** — manifestation of assent to terms; mirror-image rule at common law (last shot doctrine); **UCC §2-207** — battle-of-the-forms, additional/different terms in acceptance often included between merchants unless they materially alter, are objected to, or expressly limit.
- **Consideration** — bargained-for exchange of legal value (act, forbearance, return promise). *Hamer v. Sidway* (1891 NY) — uncle's promise of $5000 if nephew abstained from tobacco/alcohol/etc. enforceable. Past consideration insufficient; pre-existing-duty rule (*Stilk v. Myrick* 1809; modified by **UCC §2-209(1)** — modifications need no consideration in goods sales).
- **Promissory estoppel** — **Restatement §90** — promise reasonably expected to induce + does induce action or forbearance is enforceable to extent necessary to avoid injustice. *Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores* (1965 WI).

**Statute of Frauds**: certain contracts unenforceable unless evidenced by a writing signed by the party to be charged — sale of land; suretyship; in consideration of marriage; not performable within one year; **UCC §2-201** — sale of goods ≥ $500 (now adjusted in many jurisdictions).

**Parol evidence rule**: when parties reduce agreement to a final written expression, prior + contemporaneous oral/written agreements are inadmissible to contradict (integration) — distinction between **complete integration** (no extrinsic evidence at all) + **partial integration** (consistent additional terms admissible). **UCC §2-202** + Restatement §213. *Pacific Gas & Electric v. G.W. Thomas Drayage* (1968 CA, Traynor) — contextual approach.

**Interpretation + gap-filling**: ordinary meaning; reasonable expectations; *contra proferentem* (against the drafter); course of performance + course of dealing + usage of trade (**UCC §1-303**). Gap-fillers: implied warranties (merchantability **UCC §2-314**; fitness for purpose **UCC §2-315**); reasonable price; reasonable time.

**Defenses to enforcement**: **incapacity** (minors, mental incapacity); **duress** + **undue influence**; **misrepresentation** + **fraud**; **mistake** (mutual + unilateral); **unconscionability** (procedural + substantive — **Williams v. Walker-Thomas Furniture** 1965); **public policy**; **impossibility** + **impracticability** (**UCC §2-615**) + **frustration of purpose** (*Krell v. Henry* 1903 — coronation case).

**Performance + breach**: substantial performance doctrine (*Jacob & Youngs v. Kent* 1921 — Cardozo — Reading pipe vs equivalent); material breach + suspension; anticipatory repudiation (*Hochster v. De La Tour* 1853); UCC perfect-tender rule (**UCC §2-601** — sale of goods); cure right (**UCC §2-508**).

**Remedies** — three families:
- **Expectation damages** — put the plaintiff in the position as if the contract had been performed. The default.
  - **Hadley v. Baxendale (1854 Exchequer; Alderson B.)** — **foreseeability rule**: damages limited to those (1) arising naturally from the breach, or (2) reasonably contemplated by both parties at contract formation. Foundational. The miller's shipped-shaft case still controls consequential-damage analysis.
  - **Mitigation** doctrine — non-breaching party must take reasonable steps to mitigate (*Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge* 1929 — stop building the bridge).
  - **Certainty** — damages must be provable with reasonable certainty.
  - **Cost-of-completion vs diminution-in-value** (*Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal* 1962; *Jacob & Youngs*).
- **Reliance damages** — restore plaintiff to pre-contract position; alternative when expectation indeterminate.
- **Restitution** — return benefit conferred; quasi-contract recovery when no contract or upon breach (Restatement (Third) of Restitution + Unjust Enrichment 2011).
- **Specific performance** — equitable remedy ordering performance; reserved for unique subjects (land — always; goods — when unique under **UCC §2-716**); discretion + clean hands.
- **Liquidated damages** — agreed damages enforceable if (1) reasonable forecast of actual + (2) actual damages difficult to estimate; penalty clauses unenforceable.

**Third-party beneficiaries** (intended vs incidental — *Lawrence v. Fox* 1859); **assignment + delegation** (**UCC §9** secured-transactions framework + Restatement); **discharge** (performance, agreement, operation of law).

**Modern issues**: arbitration clauses + class-action waivers (*AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion* 2011; *Epic Systems v. Lewis* 2018); electronic contracting (**UETA**, **E-SIGN Act 2000**); smart contracts + blockchain-based agreements; consumer protection + unconscionability.

slides.title: Property: estates, possession, easements, zoning, + takings
slides.body:
**Property law** governs the bundle of rights people have in things (real, personal, intellectual). Common-law heritage from medieval English feudal law; modern American property is regulated by extensive state + federal overlays.

**Acquisition + possession**:
- **First possession** + capture rules — **Pierson v. Post (1805 NY)** — Pierson killed + carried off a fox that Post was pursuing; held: pursuit alone does not establish property; mortal wound or actual physical capture required. Foundational ferae naturae case; still taught.
- **Adverse possession** — open + notorious + actual + continuous + hostile (or claim of right) + exclusive possession for the statutory period (typically 10-30 years; varies by state). Color of title + payment of taxes may shorten or strengthen. Policy: quiet titles; reward productive use.
- **Gifts** — donative intent + delivery + acceptance. *Newman v. Bost* (1898 NC).
- **Lost vs mislaid vs abandoned property** — different rules (*Armory v. Delamirie* 1722 — finder of jewel against all but true owner).

**Estates in land** — the medieval system, still alive:
- **Fee simple absolute** — full + permanent ownership.
- **Defeasible fees** — fee simple determinable (auto-revert); fee simple subject to condition subsequent (right of entry); fee simple subject to executory limitation.
- **Life estate** — possession for life + remainder/reversion. Waste doctrine.
- **Future interests** — reversion; remainder (vested vs contingent); executory interest. **Rule against perpetuities** — no future interest valid unless it must vest, if at all, within 21 years after a life in being at creation. Among the hardest property doctrines; widely modified or abolished by state statute (Uniform Statutory RAP; many states now allow perpetual dynasty trusts).
- **Concurrent estates** — tenancy in common; joint tenancy with right of survivorship (4 unities — time, title, interest, possession); tenancy by the entirety (marital). Severance + partition (in kind or by sale).

**Landlord-tenant**:
- Estates — term of years; periodic tenancy; tenancy at will; tenancy at sufferance.
- **Implied warranty of habitability** (*Javins v. First National Realty* 1970 DC Cir; Skelly Wright) — modern doctrine.
- Constructive eviction; retaliatory eviction; fair-housing laws.
- COVID-era moratoria + *Alabama Association of Realtors v. HHS* (2021).

**Easements + servitudes**:
- Express + implied (prior use; necessity); easement by estoppel; easement by prescription (adverse-possession-like for use).
- Affirmative + negative; appurtenant + in gross.
- **Real covenants** + **equitable servitudes**: horizontal + vertical privity; touch + concern + notice (running with land). Modern **Restatement (Third) of Property: Servitudes** (2000) simplifies.
- **Conservation easements**: tax-favored protection of land.
- Common-interest communities (condos, HOAs).

**Zoning + land-use regulation**:
- **Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. (1926)** — Sutherland — sustained comprehensive zoning ordinance against substantive-due-process + takings challenge. **Foundational** for the entire modern zoning regime. Local police power can separate residential, commercial, industrial uses. Pigovian-style externality justification.
- **Nectow v. City of Cambridge (1928)** — as-applied takings/due-process challenges possible.
- **Mount Laurel doctrine** (1975, 1983 NJ) — exclusionary zoning + fair-share affordable-housing obligation.
- **Cluster zoning**, **PUDs**, **inclusionary zoning**, **upzoning** — modern debates over single-family-only zoning + housing supply (Minneapolis, Oregon, California SB 9 + SB 10).
- **Historic preservation** (*Penn Central v. New York City* 1978).

**Takings — the Fifth Amendment**: 'nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.' Incorporated against states via the Fourteenth (*Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R.R. v. Chicago* 1897).
- **Physical takings** — *Loretto v. Teleprompter Manhattan CATV* (1982) — even a tiny physical occupation (cable box on apartment building) is a per se taking.
- **Public-use requirement** — **Kelo v. City of New London (2005)** — Stevens — economic-development redevelopment is a 'public use' under broad reading; sustained New London's transfer of homes to private developer (project later failed). Triggered nationwide backlash + state-law eminent-domain reform (legislative + constitutional).
- **Regulatory takings**:
  - **Pennsylvania Coal Co. v. Mahon (1922)** — Holmes — 'if a regulation goes too far it will be recognized as a taking.' First major regulatory-takings doctrine.
  - **Penn Central v. New York City (1978)** — Brennan — three-factor test for regulatory takings: (1) economic impact; (2) interference with distinct investment-backed expectations; (3) character of governmental action. Ad-hoc + factual.
  - **Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992)** — Scalia — categorical rule: regulation that **denies all economically beneficial use** of land is a per se taking, unless background principles of state property/nuisance law would have prohibited the use anyway.
  - **Nollan v. California Coastal Commission (1987)** + **Dolan v. City of Tigard (1994)** + **Koontz v. St. Johns River Water Management District (2013)** — essential-nexus + rough-proportionality test for exactions; permit conditions must be linked + proportional to the project's impacts.
  - **Murr v. Wisconsin (2017)** — multi-factor parcel-as-a-whole analysis.
- **Just compensation** — fair market value at time of taking; severance damages; physical occupation easier than regulatory.

**Intellectual property** is property too (covered in business-law-and-regulation): patents (35 U.S.C.), copyrights (17 U.S.C.), trademarks (Lanham Act), trade secrets (DTSA 2016).

slides.title: Torts: negligence, products liability, + defamation
slides.body:
**Tort law** = civil wrongs other than breach of contract, redressed by damages (mostly). Three families:

**Negligence** — the dominant tort. Five elements:
1. **Duty** — legally cognizable obligation to conform to a standard of care. Default: reasonable-person-in-like-circumstances. Special relationships (innkeeper-guest; common carrier-passenger; landowner-entrant; professional-client).
2. **Breach** — failure to meet the standard. **Learned Hand's BPL formula** — *United States v. Carroll Towing Co.* (1947, 2d Cir.) — **B < PL** = breach when burden of precaution (B) is less than probability of harm (P) × magnitude of harm (L). Cost-benefit framing that influenced law-and-economics (Posner).
3. **Causation**:
   - **Actual cause** — but-for cause (or substantial-factor when multiple causes).
   - **Proximate cause** — foreseeable scope of risk. **Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad (1928)** — Cardozo (majority) — duty owed only to plaintiffs within the foreseeable zone of risk; Andrews (dissent) — broader 'proximate cause' inquiry. Iconic — taught in every torts course. The fireworks-package-distant-scales injury at LIRR's East New York station crystallizes the doctrine.
4. **Damages** — actual harm (physical, property, emotional + economic in limited contexts).
5. **Defenses** — comparative negligence (modified majority; pure in some states); contributory negligence (only AL, MD, NC, VA, DC); assumption of risk (express + implied; primary + secondary); statutory immunities.

**Standards of care**:
- Reasonable-person standard (objective).
- Professional standard (medical malpractice — local + national standard debate; informed consent).
- Children — age-graded; adult activities held to adult standard.
- Mental disability generally not a defense to negligence (per *Vaughan v. Menlove* 1837; *Bashi v. Wodarz* 1996 CA).
- **Res ipsa loquitur** — 'the thing speaks for itself'; circumstantial inference of negligence (*Byrne v. Boadle* 1863 — flour-barrel falling from second-story window).
- **Negligence per se** — violation of safety statute can establish breach (Restatement (Third) Torts: Liability for Physical + Emotional Harm §14).

**Strict liability** — liability without fault for abnormally dangerous activities (*Rylands v. Fletcher* 1868 — reservoir burst) + animals (wild animals; trespassing livestock).

**Products liability** — modern: **Greenman v. Yuba Power Products (1963)** — California — strict liability of manufacturers for defective products; **Restatement (Second) of Torts §402A (1965)** — strict liability for products in defective condition unreasonably dangerous; **Restatement (Third) Torts: Products Liability (1998)** — three defect categories: manufacturing defect, design defect (risk-utility + consumer-expectations tests), warning defect. Asbestos, tobacco, pharma, opioid litigation. **State Farm v. Campbell (2003)** + **Philip Morris v. Williams (2007)** — punitive-damage limits (single-digit ratios, due-process constraints).

**Intentional torts**:
- **Battery** — intentional harmful/offensive contact.
- **Assault** — apprehension of imminent battery.
- **False imprisonment**; **IIED** (intentional infliction of emotional distress — *outrageous* conduct).
- **Trespass** to land + chattels; **conversion**.

**Defamation** — libel (written) + slander (oral). Common-law elements: defamatory statement + of + or concerning plaintiff + publication to third party + (today) fault + damages.
- **New York Times v. Sullivan (1964)** — Brennan unanimous — public-official plaintiffs must prove **actual malice** (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard) by **clear + convincing** evidence. Foundational. **Curtis Publishing v. Butts (1967)** extended to public figures. **Gertz v. Robert Welch (1974)** + **Dun & Bradstreet v. Greenmoss (1985)** — private-figure framework; states may set standard but no presumed damages without fault.
- **Anti-SLAPP statutes** (CA + many states) — strike suits aimed at chilling speech.
- **Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996)** — Internet platforms not liable as publishers for user content; under active reform debate.
- *Hustler Magazine v. Falwell* (1988) — Rehnquist — public-figure IIED requires actual malice for false-statement liability.

**Privacy torts** (Prosser's four — *Privacy* 48 Cal. L. Rev. 383 (1960)): intrusion; public disclosure of private facts; false light; appropriation/right of publicity.

**Damages**:
- **Compensatory** — economic (medical, lost wages, future earnings — discounted to present value; Bureau of Labor Statistics; structured settlements); non-economic (pain + suffering — many states cap); property.
- **Punitive** — punishment + deterrence; *BMW v. Gore* (1996); *State Farm v. Campbell* (2003) — single-digit ratio guidance.
- **Caps + tort reform** — many states cap noneconomic + total damages; periodic state constitutional challenges.
- **Joint + several liability** — apportionment statutes vary widely.
- **Collateral source rule** — payments from independent sources do not reduce damages (eroded by many state reforms).

**Mass torts** — asbestos (millions of claims; bankruptcies — Manville Trust; § 524(g) channeling); tobacco (Master Settlement Agreement 1998 — $206B+ over 25 years); opioids (~$50B settlement framework with states/locals 2021-22); 3M earplugs (largest MDL in case count); pharma (Vioxx, Mirena, talc).

Torts allocate the cost of accidents + intentional harms across the economy + the social fabric. It is also the principal common-law arena in which judges still make law freely + Posner's law-and-economics frame has most influence.

question.question: Apply Hadley v. Baxendale + the foreseeability rule
question.goal: A miller's crank-shaft breaks; he contracts with a carrier for prompt delivery to engineers for replacement. The carrier delays. The mill is shut down longer; lost profits substantial. Apply Hadley v. Baxendale.

steps.prompt: What is the Hadley v Baxendale (1854) rule?

acceptedAnswers: Damages limited to those (1) arising naturally + in the usual course from breach, or (2) reasonably contemplated by both parties at formation (foreseeability rule)

steps.reveal: **Hadley v. Baxendale (1854)** — Alderson B. — damages recoverable for breach are those (1) arising naturally + according to the usual course of things from the breach itself, or (2) such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time they made the contract as the probable result of the breach. Limits consequential damages to foreseeable + communicated risks.

steps.prompt: Were the lost profits foreseeable in Hadley v Baxendale itself?

acceptedAnswers: The court held lost profits were not recoverable because the carrier did not know that the mill was shut down for want of the shaft — it was not communicated + thus not within the contemplation of both parties

hints: Did the carrier know the mill was shut down?
steps.reveal: The Exchequer held: the lost profits were not recoverable. The carrier did not know the mill was shut down + waiting for the shaft; absent that special knowledge, the loss was not in the parties' reasonable contemplation. Holmes + later courts: the rule incentivizes information disclosure at formation — promisees who want consequential-damage protection must signal the risk.

steps.prompt: How would the analysis change today under UCC §2-715 or Restatement (Second) §351?

acceptedAnswers: Restatement §351 + UCC §2-715 codify Hadley but allow consequential damages if seller had reason to know of special needs; modern tort + contract doctrine refines foreseeability

steps.reveal: **Restatement (Second) §351** + **UCC §2-715(2)** codify foreseeability + allow consequential damages when the breaching party had reason to know of buyer's particular needs or general or particular requirements. **UCC §2-719** — parties may limit/exclude consequentials, subject to unconscionability + failure of essential purpose. Modern contracts almost always have consequential-damage waivers.

steps.prompt: How does Hadley v Baxendale fit Posner's law-and-economics frame?

acceptedAnswers: Posner: Hadley = optimal information-disclosure rule; promisees with high-stakes incentivized to disclose so promisor can price + take precautions

steps.reveal: **Posner** (Economic Analysis of Law) reads Hadley as an **information-forcing default**: by limiting damages to foreseeable losses, the rule induces promisees with unusual risk to disclose at formation so promisor can adjust price/precaution. Allocates risk efficiently + encourages optimal precaution. A canonical law-and-economics application — the Coase-Posner frame in action.

question.question: Why are Euclid (1926), Kelo (2005), + Lucas (1992) the three pillars of modern land-use + takings doctrine?
options: **Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. (1926)** — Sutherland — sustained comprehensive zoning against substantive-due-process + takings challenge; foundational green light for the entire modern American zoning regime. Local police power permits separating residential/commercial/industrial uses (Pigovian externality framing). Without *Euclid*, modern American land use would be unrecognizable. **Kelo v. City of New London (2005)** — Stevens — sustained eminent-domain transfer of homes to a private developer for economic-development redevelopment as 'public use' under the broad-reading approach. Triggered nationwide backlash + state-law eminent-domain reform (~40 states tightened in the years following). Continues to be litigated + reformed. **Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992)** — Scalia — categorical rule: a regulation that **denies all economically beneficial use** of land is a per se taking unless background principles of state property/nuisance law would have prohibited the use. Carved out from the *Penn Central* (1978) ad-hoc three-factor test. Together: **Euclid** authorizes zoning; **Kelo** defines public-use limits + triggered reform; **Lucas** sets the per-se regulatory-taking threshold. They structure the entire American constitutional framework for land regulation.
question.explanation: Euclid (1926, zoning sustained), Kelo (2005, broad public use sustained + reform backlash), Lucas (1992, per-se takings when all economically beneficial use denied) — together they structure modern American land-use + takings doctrine.

slides.workedSolution: Euclid (1926) authorizes zoning under police power. Kelo (2005) sustained broad public-use eminent domain (triggered state reforms). Lucas (1992) per se taking when all economically beneficial use denied. Together: zoning + eminent domain + regulatory takings architecture.

question.question: A defective product + media coverage — torts + defamation overlap
question.prompt: A manufacturer's product fails + injures consumers. A major newspaper publishes an investigative story stating the manufacturer 'knowingly hid' the defect; the manufacturer claims this is false + sues for defamation. (a) Apply **strict products liability** (Restatement Third §1-2) + **negligence** + **Learned Hand BPL formula** to the consumer claims. (b) Walk through **Palsgraf** zone-of-risk + proximate cause. (c) For the defamation claim, identify whether the manufacturer is a **public figure** + apply **New York Times v. Sullivan (1964)** + **Gertz (1974)** — actual-malice requirement, clear-+-convincing burden. (d) Discuss the **Section 230** exposure of online platforms republishing the story + the anti-SLAPP framework. (e) Predict how **Hadley v. Baxendale** would limit any contract claims between manufacturer + distributors + how punitive-damage limits (**State Farm v. Campbell**) cap the verdict.

question.question: Learned Hand's BPL formula — write the condition for negligence breach.
question.hint: Carroll Towing 1947 (Learned Hand, 2d Cir.): negligence when Burden of precaution < Probability × Loss.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the architecture of private law: contracts + property + torts.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Contracts** — offer + acceptance + consideration; **UCC Article 2** (Llewellyn) for goods; promissory estoppel; **parol evidence rule**; **Hadley v Baxendale** (1854, Alderson B.) foreseeability + consequential damages; mitigation; specific performance for unique items + land. **Property** — **Pierson v Post** (1805) first possession; adverse possession; estates + future interests + RAP; easements + servitudes; **Euclid v Ambler** (1926) zoning; **Kelo** (2005) public use; takings (**Penn Central** 1978 + **Lucas** 1992 per se rule + **Nollan/Dolan/Koontz** exactions). **Torts** — negligence's duty/breach/causation/damages; **Learned Hand BPL** (Carroll Towing 1947); **Palsgraf** (1928, Cardozo) zone of risk; **Greenman** + Restatement §402A products liability; **New York Times v Sullivan** (1964, Brennan) defamation actual malice for public officials/figures; punitive-damage caps. Concludes: private law is the day-to-day operating system of voluntary exchange + accident allocation.
